cards.front: Name the two cyclooxygenase isoforms and the role of each.
cards.back: COX-1 is constitutive and maintains housekeeping functions such as gastric mucosal protection and platelet TXA2. COX-2 is induced by cytokines at inflamed sites and drives local prostaglandin generation. COX-2 is also present constitutively in brain, juxtaglomerular cells and the foetus.

cards.front: Classify: NSAIDs by chemical class
cards.text: Ibuprofen and naproxen are {{propionic acid}} derivatives; ketorolac and indomethacin are {{acetic acid}} derivatives; piroxicam and tenoxicam are {{oxicams}}; mephenamic acid is a {{fenamate}}; paracetamol is a {{para-aminophenol}}; propyphenazone is a {{pyrazolone}}; nefopam is a {{benzoxazocine}}.

cards.front: Classify: NSAID adverse effects by system
cards.text: Renal: {{sodium and water retention}} and {{papillary necrosis}}; hepatic: {{raised transaminases}}; CNS: {{tinnitus}} and {{confusion}}; haematological: {{thrombocytopenia}} and {{haemolytic anaemia}}; respiratory: {{asthma}} in aspirin-sensitive patients.

cards.front: Classify: drugs used to close a patent ductus arteriosus
cards.text: Ductus arteriosus is kept open by {{PGE2}} made by {{COX-2}}; after birth it closes naturally, but if it does not, small doses of {{indomethacin}} or {{aspirin}} close it by blocking PG synthesis.

cards.front: Why can indomethacin or aspirin close a patent ductus arteriosus, and why should NSAIDs be avoided near term?
cards.back: Foetal ductus is held open by PGE2 made by COX-2. Blocking PG synthesis lets it close, so indomethacin or aspirin is used when it fails to shut after birth. The same effect late in pregnancy can close the ductus prematurely and raises post-partum bleeding risk.

cards.front: Which NSAID suits each situation: mild pain, post-operative pain, renal colic, RA flare?
cards.back: Mild pain with little inflammation: paracetamol or low-dose ibuprofen. Short post-operative pain: injectable ketorolac or diclofenac, or oral propionic acid derivative or nimesulide. Parenteral NSAID for renal colic or acute gout: ketorolac, diclofenac or parecoxib. RA or gout flare: naproxen, piroxicam, indomethacin or high-dose aspirin. Reason: pain-to-inflammation ratio and patient risk drive the pick.

cards.front: Essay: NSAIDs - classification, mechanism and adverse effects

points: Analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory actions in varying measure
Non-opioid: no CNS depression, no dependence or abuse liability
Mainly peripheral action, with a central component
Inhibition of cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis
COX-1 governs housekeeping; COX-2 governs inflammatory PGs
Aspirin is irreversible; most others are reversible
Antipyresis by blocking hypothalamic PGE2 from pyrogens
Salicylates: aspirin
Propionic acids: ibuprofen, naproxen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen
Fenamate: mephenamic acid
Enolic acids (oxicams): piroxicam, tenoxicam
Acetic acids: ketorolac, indomethacin, nabumetone (prodrug)
Pyrazolone: propyphenazone
Preferential COX-2 inhibitors: nimesulide, diclofenac, aceclofenac, meloxicam, etodolac
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs): celecoxib, etoricoxib, parecoxib
Analgesic-antipyretics with poor anti-inflammatory action: paracetamol (para-aminophenol), nefopam (benzoxazocine)
GI: erosions, ulcers, bleeding
Renal: sodium and water retention, reduced GFR, papillary necrosis
Platelet inhibition and bleeding
Asthma and anaphylactoid reactions in susceptible patients

Efficacy differences are minor; side-effect profiles differ
Choose by pain type, inflammation, risk factors and past response
Analgesic combinations offer no clear advantage

cards.front: How does aspirin inhibit COX differently from most other NSAIDs?
cards.back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue of COX irreversibly, so activity returns only when new enzyme is synthesised. Most other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible; their effect ends when the drug dissociates from the enzyme.

cards.front: Classify: key facts about aspirin
cards.text: Aspirin is converted to {{salicylic acid}}; its antiplatelet effect results from {{irreversible}} acetylation of COX-1 and lasts about {{one week}}; low-dose secondary prevention uses {{75 to 150 mg}} daily; analgesic doses are {{0.3 to 0.6 g}} every 6 to 8 hours.

cards.front: What is salicylism and at what aspirin dose does it appear?
cards.back: Syndrome from anti-inflammatory doses (3 to 5 g/day): dizziness, tinnitus, vertigo, reversible hearing and vision impairment, excitement, hyperventilation and electrolyte imbalance. Tinnitus is the classic early warning that the dose is too high.

cards.front: Why does a low daily dose of aspirin protect platelets for about a week, while ibuprofen's antiplatelet effect is short?
cards.back: Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX-1 and hence TXA2 synthesis. Platelets cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts about a week, the platelet lifespan. Ibuprofen binds reversibly and its effect is short lived.

cards.front: What happens when ibuprofen is taken with low-dose aspirin?
cards.back: Ibuprofen occupies the active site of platelet COX-1 reversibly, so aspirin cannot acetylate it. This abolishes aspirin's antiplatelet and cardioprotective effect, so ibuprofen should not be used in patients relying on aspirin for cardioprotection.

cards.front: Short note: Aspirin as an antiplatelet agent

points: Irreversible acetylation of platelet COX-1
Blocks TXA2 synthesis, so aggregation falls
Effect lasts about a week (platelet lifespan)
Low doses of 75 to 150 mg/day are enough for antiplatelet effect
High doses also suppress endothelial PGI2, which can cancel the benefit
Secondary prevention after MI, stroke or TIA
New-onset or unstable angina
Pre-eclampsia prevention at 80 to 100 mg/day from the 12th week
Prolonged bleeding time
Added bleeding risk with anticoagulants
Stop about one week before elective surgery

cards.front: Short note: Acute salicylate poisoning

points: Children are more vulnerable
Fatal dose in adults is estimated at 15 to 30 g
Elimination becomes saturated, so toxicity rises steeply
Vomiting, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Mixed acid-base disorder: early respiratory alkalosis, later acidosis
Hyperpyrexia, delirium, convulsions and coma
Death from respiratory failure and circulatory collapse
Symptomatic and supportive care
External cooling for hyperpyrexia
IV fluids with Na+, K+, bicarbonate and glucose, guided by repeated monitoring
Blood transfusion and vitamin K if bleeding occurs

cards.front: Essay: Aspirin - pharmacology, uses and toxicity

Analgesic at 0.3 to 0.6 g every 6 to 8 hours; maximal analgesia near 1 g

Anti-inflammatory at high doses of 3 to 6 g/day
Uncouples oxidative phosphorylation and raises metabolism
Respiratory stimulation, then alkalosis; toxic doses cause acidosis
Blunts the uricosuric action of probenecid
Absorbed from stomach and small intestine; poor solubility limits absorption
About 80% protein bound

GI erosion and occult blood loss

Hypersensitivity and asthma; Reye's syndrome in children

cards.front: Short note: Current therapeutic status of aspirin

points: Rarely used now as an anti-inflammatory drug
Paracetamol is generally preferred as the safer analgesic-antipyretic
Less effective than other NSAIDs in ankylosing spondylitis
Low daily dose irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 for the platelet lifespan
Secondary prevention after MI, stroke, TIA and unstable angina; also after bypass graft
Reduces serious vascular events by about 20 to 25% in high-risk patients
Recent trials in primary prevention showed no clear benefit
GI bleeding risk remains and can offset gains
Long-term use is linked to lower colorectal cancer risk in epidemiological studies
Avoid in children with viral infections (Reye syndrome)
Ibuprofen given concurrently blocks aspirin antiplatelet action

cards.front: What paracetamol dose signals serious toxicity, and when is fatality likely?
cards.back: KDT: above about 150 mg/kg (over 10 g in an adult) can cause serious toxicity, and fatality is common above about 250 mg/kg. GG14: hepatotoxicity may follow a single 10 to 15 g (150 to 250 mg/kg) in adults or more than 150 mg/kg in children; 20 to 25 g or more is potentially fatal. Alcoholics and fasting or malnourished patients are at risk at lower doses. Early features are only nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; centrilobular necrosis develops after 12 to 18 hours, clinical liver damage shows in 2 to 4 days, and transaminases peak at 72 to 96 hours.

cards.front: Which analgesic-antipyretic is safest in pregnancy, and why is aspirin avoided in children with viral infections?
cards.back: Paracetamol is the safest choice in pregnancy, with low-dose aspirin probably second best. Aspirin is avoided in children with varicella or influenza because of its link with Reye's syndrome, a rare hepatic encephalopathy; paediatric aspirin formulations are prohibited in India and the UK.

cards.front: What does paracetamol lack compared with aspirin, and where is it used?
cards.back: It has negligible anti-inflammatory action, does not affect platelets, clotting, gastric mucosa, respiration or acid-base balance, and is not uricosuric. Used for headache, mild migraine, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhoea, first-choice analgesic in osteoarthritis and antipyretic for fever, especially in children (no Reye risk). It is weak where inflammation dominates, e.g. RA.

cards.front: Why is paracetamol a good antipyretic but a poor anti-inflammatory drug?
cards.back: It is a weak inhibitor of peripheral COX. Peroxides generated at inflamed sites block its action there, but no such peroxides are present in the brain, where it inhibits COX well. Action on the brain isoform COX-3 may also contribute.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of paracetamol-induced hepatic injury?
cards.back: A minor oxidative metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NABQI), is normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. After a very large dose, glucuronidation saturates, more NABQI forms and hepatic glutathione is depleted. NABQI then binds liver and renal tubular proteins, causing necrosis.

cards.front: Paracetamol poisoning: antidote, how it works, and the dosing regimen.
cards.back: N-acetylcysteine (NAC). It replenishes hepatic glutathione and can also conjugate NAPQI directly, so the toxic metabolite is detoxified instead of binding liver proteins. Standard regimen (GG12): IV 150 mg/kg over 60 min, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h; or oral 140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses. KDT gives a simpler scheme: 150 mg/kg IV over 15 min, then the same dose over 20 h, or 75 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 h for 2 to 3 days. Start before blood levels return if overdose is suspected; given within 8 to 16 h, mortality falls below 1%, but it is practically ineffective if started 16 h or later. Side effects: rash, nausea, vomiting, rare anaphylactoid reactions.

cards.front: Essay: Paracetamol - pharmacology, toxicity and management

points: Central analgesic and antipyretic with negligible peripheral anti-inflammatory action
No effect on platelets, clotting, acid-base balance or CVS
Not uricosuric
Well absorbed orally; about 25% protein bound
Conjugated with glucuronic acid and sulfate
Plasma half-life 2 to 3 hours
Headache, mild migraine, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhoea
Preferred antipyretic in children and pregnancy
Preferred over aspirin in ulcer patients and where aspirin is contraindicated
At risk: young children, alcoholics (CYP2E1 induction), fasting or malnourished patients, overdose
NAPQI formation and glutathione depletion
Hepatic necrosis at 12 to 18 hours; jaundice by about day 2; transaminases peak at 72 to 96 hours
Renal tubular necrosis and hypoglycaemia may occur
Activated charcoal within 4 hours of ingestion cuts absorption by 50 to 90%; gastric lavage is generally not recommended (GG12)
N-acetylcysteine, most effective when started early; do not wait for blood levels
Supportive care for hepatic and renal failure; monitor glucose
Fulminant hepatic failure: liver transplantation

cards.front: Classify: selective COX-2 inhibitors
cards.text: Among the coxibs, {{etoricoxib}} has the highest COX-2 selectivity and is given once daily; {{celecoxib}} is metabolised mainly by {{CYP2C9}}; {{parecoxib}} is an injectable prodrug of {{valdecoxib}}.

cards.front: Compare celecoxib and etoricoxib: COX-2 selectivity and key points.
cards.back: Celecoxib is only modestly COX-2 selective (about 10-fold), as effective as naproxen or diclofenac in RA, spares platelet COX-1 and gastric mucosa; side effects are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, rash, oedema and small BP rise. Etoricoxib has the highest selectivity, half-life about 24 h so once daily, and thrombotic CV event rate similar to diclofenac.

cards.front: What is parecoxib, and what hazard does it share with valdecoxib?
cards.back: Parecoxib is an injectable prodrug of valdecoxib for post-operative or similar short-term pain, with efficacy like ketorolac. It shares valdecoxib's risk of serious skin reactions, so stop it at the first rash.

cards.front: Why were rofecoxib and valdecoxib withdrawn?
cards.back: Both were linked to increased myocardial infarction. Rofecoxib was stopped in the APPROVE trial and withdrawn globally in 2004; valdecoxib was withdrawn in 2005 after cardiac events in patients undergoing bypass surgery, and also because of severe skin reactions.

cards.front: What are the main safety concerns with nimesulide, and where is it still specifically useful?
cards.back: It can cause fulminant hepatic failure and has been withdrawn in several countries; its use in children is banned in India. Its specific value lies in patients with asthma or aspirin intolerance, most of whom do not cross-react with it.

cards.front: Short note: Selective COX-2 inhibitors and cardiovascular risk

points: COX-2 inhibitors lower endothelial PGI2 without reducing platelet TXA2
The imbalance favours thrombosis
VIGOR: about four-fold more MI with rofecoxib than naproxen
APPROVE: rofecoxib stopped early and withdrawn in 2004
APC trial: about 2.5-fold more major CV events with celecoxib
CLASS trial: no excess CV events with celecoxib
Valdecoxib withdrawn in 2005
Lumiracoxib suspended for hepatotoxicity
US committee in 2005 favoured a CV warning rather than blanket withdrawal
Avoid in ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, heart failure and cerebrovascular disease
Do not combine with low-dose aspirin, as GI injury increases
Lowest dose for the shortest period

cards.front: Case: RA patient with a past peptic ulcer and hypertension needs an NSAID. Reason out the choice.
cards.back: Gastric risk argues for a COX-2 selective drug (or paracetamol), or a traditional NSAID with a PPI. But hypertension and CV risk argue against coxibs, which lack antiplatelet action and give a small BP rise. So the lowest dose for the shortest time of a propionic acid derivative such as naproxen (lower thrombotic risk than diclofenac or etoricoxib) plus a PPI is the balanced answer; consider a DMARD to cut NSAID need.

cards.front: List the main mechanisms of NSAID-induced gastric mucosal injury.
cards.back: Loss of COX-1-derived protective PGE2 and PGI2 reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increases acid secretion and reduces mucosal blood flow. Back-diffusion of H+ ions in the mucosa adds to the damage. Misoprostol, a stable PG analogue, counteracts NSAID gastric toxicity.

cards.front: Which COX product loss causes NSAID gastric damage?
cards.back: Inhibition of COX-1 derived PGE2 and PGI2, the gastroprotective prostaglandins. Without them mucus and bicarbonate fall, acid rises and mucosal blood flow drops, so erosion and ulcer follow.

cards.front: What gastroprotection is used when an NSAID-dependent arthritis patient develops a peptic ulcer?
cards.back: Concurrent proton pump inhibitor. Alternatives for gastric intolerance or predisposed patients: a selective COX-2 inhibitor or paracetamol.

cards.front: Which analgesics have been adequately evaluated in children, and which to avoid?
cards.back: Only paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen and naproxen are well studied in children. Avoid aspirin because of Reye's syndrome, so paracetamol is preferred for fever.

cards.front: Short note: Gastric toxicity of NSAIDs

points: Loss of COX-1 PGs (PGE2, PGI2)
Less mucus and bicarbonate, more acid secretion
Reduced mucosal blood flow
Back-diffusion of H+ ions in the mucosa
Dyspepsia, erosions and peptic ulcer
Bleeding and perforation
Aspirin ion-trapping in mucosal cells adds to injury
Occult blood loss even after a single aspirin tablet
Co-prescribe misoprostol, a stable PG analogue
Proton pump inhibitor for patients with ulcer history on NSAIDs
Selective COX-2 inhibitor or paracetamol for intolerant patients
Buffered or soluble aspirin does not significantly reduce ulcers

cards.front: Short note: Choosing an NSAID in special patients

points: Only paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen and naproxen are well studied
Avoid aspirin because of Reye's syndrome
Paracetamol is the safest
Low-dose aspirin is probably second best
NSAIDs should be avoided near term
Nimesulide or a selective COX-2 inhibitor
Most aspirin-sensitive asthmatics do not cross-react with nimesulide
Avoid selective COX-2 inhibitors
Use a propionic acid derivative or aspirin at the lowest dose

cards.front: Case: elderly asthmatic with aspirin sensitivity and gastric intolerance has osteoarthritis pain. Choose analgesia.
cards.back: Paracetamol first (first-choice for OA, minimal gastric effect, no aspirin cross-reactivity). If an NSAID is needed, nimesulide or a COX-2 inhibitor suits aspirin-sensitive asthma and gastric risk, at a reduced elderly dose, with PPI cover if ulcer history; note nimesulide hepatotoxicity concerns and ban in children.

cards.front: What is a DMARD, and how does it differ from an NSAID?
cards.back: A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug suppresses the rheumatoid process and slows progression. Unlike NSAIDs it has no nonspecific anti-inflammatory or analgesic action. Benefit takes months to appear, and relapse occurs after stopping.

cards.front: What is sulfasalazine made of, and what is its role in RA?
cards.back: It is sulfapyridine linked to 5-aminosalicylic acid. In RA it is a second-line or add-on DMARD of modest efficacy. Neutropenia or thrombocytopenia occurs in about 5 to 10% of patients, so blood counts need monitoring.

cards.front: Classify: non-biological DMARDs
cards.text: Non-biological DMARDs include {{methotrexate}}, {{sulfasalazine}}, {{hydroxychloroquine}}, {{leflunomide}}, {{azathioprine}} and the JAK inhibitor {{tofacitinib}}.

cards.front: Why is methotrexate the first-choice DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis, and how does it act?
cards.back: It is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that reduces proliferation of immune-inflammatory cells and cytokine production. Relief starts in 3 to 6 weeks, response is predictable and sustained, and the weekly oral low dose (7.5 to 15 mg) is well accepted. It is standard even in juvenile RA.

cards.front: What are the serious toxicities of methotrexate, and when is it contraindicated?
cards.back: Oral ulceration and GI upset are common. Prolonged use causes dose-related liver damage progressing to cirrhosis, and chest infections increase. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, breast-feeding, liver disease, active infection, leucopenia and peptic ulcer, and is avoided in renal disease because excretion is impaired.

cards.front: Which drugs increase methotrexate levels or toxicity?
cards.back: Aspirin and probenecid raise methotrexate levels by reducing its excretion. Trimethoprim adds to dihydrofolate reductase inhibition and can depress bone marrow.

cards.front: Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred over chloroquine when used in RA?
cards.back: Both take 3 to 6 months to act and do not prevent bony erosions. Retinal damage and corneal opacity are the main concern; these are less frequent and reversible with hydroxychloroquine. It is best reserved for mild, non-erosive disease.

cards.front: How does leflunomide act, and why is a loading dose needed?
cards.back: It is converted to an active metabolite that inhibits dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in dividing cells. The metabolite has a half-life of 2 to 3 weeks, so a loading dose of 100 mg daily for 3 days precedes 20 mg daily. It must not be used in pregnancy or children.

cards.front: What is the main use of azathioprine in RA, and what interaction limits its dose?
cards.back: It is converted to 6-mercaptopurine and is used mainly for its steroid-sparing effect, especially in systemic disease. It is not combined with methotrexate. Allopurinol inhibits its breakdown, so the azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine dose is cut to about one-third.

Weekly oral dose of 7.5 to 15 mg
Symptom relief in 3 to 6 weeks
Standard first-line DMARD, including juvenile RA

Pregnancy, breast-feeding, liver disease, active infection, leucopenia, peptic ulcer

cards.front: Short note: Hydroxychloroquine in rheumatoid arthritis

points: Antimalarial; exact mechanism in RA is unknown

Mild, non-erosive disease, or one or a few joints
Combined with methotrexate or sulfasalazine when needed
Induces remission in up to about half of patients over 3 to 6 months
400 mg/day for 4 to 6 weeks, then 200 mg/day for maintenance
Retinal damage and corneal opacity; less with hydroxychloroquine than chloroquine
Rashes, hair greying, GI upset, myopathy and neuropathy

cards.front: JAK inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis: mechanism, agents and key adverse effects.
cards.back: Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) are tyrosine kinases activated by cytokine receptors; they phosphorylate STAT transcription factors that switch on inflammatory genes. Oral JAK inhibitors block this signalling and cytokine production. Tofacitinib (JAK1/JAK3, 5 mg twice daily) is used in severe RA not responding to methotrexate, alone or with methotrexate, but not with azathioprine, cyclosporine or biological DMARDs. Other JAK inhibitors approved for RA include baricitinib (JAK1/JAK2) and upadacitinib (JAK1). Adverse effects: respiratory infections, reactivation of tuberculosis, headache, diarrhoea, hypertension, anaemia and liver damage. GG14: a boxed warning covers serious infections, malignancy, thrombosis, major cardiovascular events and death, and since 2021 the US label limits them to patients who respond poorly to TNF antagonists.

Low-dose prednisolone (5 to 7.5 mg) as a bridge; long-term steroid dependence is a problem
Intra-articular steroid for one or a few joints, not repeated before 3 to 4 months
Start a DMARD as soon as RA is confirmed
Methotrexate is the usual first choice
Add sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine or leflunomide as needed
Advanced cases may need two or three DMARDs together
Biologics such as TNF inhibitors, abatacept, anakinra and rituximab for refractory disease
Tofacitinib for severe disease not responding to methotrexate

Benefit takes months; relapse follows withdrawal
First-line, rapid onset of 3 to 6 weeks
Weekly oral low dose; toxicity includes liver damage and oral ulcers
Leflunomide: pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor with long-acting metabolite
Tofacitinib: JAK inhibitor for severe methotrexate non-responders, not combined with azathioprine or biologics
Sulfasalazine: second-line, neutropenia monitoring
Hydroxychloroquine: milder disease; retinal toxicity
Steroid-sparing agent, not combined with methotrexate
Dose limited by allopurinol interaction
Methotrexate forms the base of most combinations
Individual drugs chosen by disease severity, erosions and tolerance

cards.front: How do TNF inhibitors work, and what is their main hazard?
cards.back: They neutralise TNF, either as a soluble receptor or an antibody, reducing macrophage and T-cell activation. They act faster than conventional DMARDs and slow erosions. The main hazard is opportunistic infection, including tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia, because TNF is needed against granulomatous infection.

cards.front: Classify: biologic DMARDs by target
cards.text: TNF inhibitors: {{etanercept}}, {{infliximab}}, {{adalimumab}}, {{certolizumab}} and {{golimumab}}; IL-1 blocker: {{anakinra}}; T-cell costimulation blocker: {{abatacept}}; anti-CD20 B-cell depleter: {{rituximab}}.

cards.front: Name the TNF inhibitors and their type.
cards.back: Etanercept (TNF-receptor/Fc fusion protein), infliximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody), adalimumab (human monoclonal antibody), plus certolizumab and golimumab. They are reserve drugs for severe refractory RA, usually added to methotrexate, which lowers antibody formation against infliximab and adalimumab.

cards.front: How does abatacept act, and with which drug must it not be combined?
cards.back: It is a CTLA-4 Fc fusion protein that binds CD80 and CD86, blocking the second costimulatory signal needed for T-cell activation. It is used in active RA not responding to methotrexate. It must not be combined with TNF antagonists because infection risk rises greatly.

cards.front: Short note: Biological DMARDs in rheumatoid arthritis

points: Recombinant proteins or monoclonal antibodies against TNF, IL-1 or T-cell costimulation
Reserved for severe or refractory disease because they are expensive
Etanercept: TNF receptor-Fc fusion protein, subcutaneous
Infliximab: chimeric monoclonal antibody, IV every 4 to 8 weeks
Adalimumab: human anti-TNF antibody, subcutaneous every 2 weeks
Anakinra: IL-1 receptor antagonist
Abatacept and rituximab for selected refractory cases
Opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia
Infusion reactions with infliximab
Worsening heart failure with infliximab
Injection-site reactions
TNF inhibitors are usually given with methotrexate, which reduces antibody formation
Abatacept is not combined with TNF antagonists

cards.front: Case: RA not controlled by methotrexate plus a TNF inhibitor. What next and what to avoid?
cards.back: Options are abatacept (blocks CD80/CD86 costimulation of T cells) or rituximab (B-cell depletion) with methotrexate; anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) is rarely used. Never combine abatacept with a TNF antagonist (very high infection risk). Screen for TB beforehand since TNF blockade flares granulomatous infection.

cards.front: Classify: drugs for an acute gout attack
cards.text: Options are {{NSAIDs}} at high dose, {{colchicine}} (fastest but more toxic), intra-articular {{soluble corticosteroid}} for one or a few joints, and systemic {{prednisolone}} when NSAIDs and colchicine are unsuitable.

cards.front: Classify: urate-lowering drugs by mechanism
cards.text: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors: {{allopurinol}} and {{febuxostat}}; uricosurics: {{probenecid}}, {{lesinurad}} and the largely disused {{sulfinpyrazone}}; uricase enzyme: {{pegloticase}}.

cards.front: How does probenecid lower blood uric acid, and what are its limits?
cards.back: It blocks URAT-1 (an organic acid transporter) so tubular reabsorption of urate falls and excretion rises. Ineffective in renal insufficiency, avoid in stone formers (give fluids), and aspirin blocks its effect. Cover the first 1 to 2 months with NSAID or colchicine to avoid precipitating acute gout.

cards.front: How does colchicine act in acute gout, and what limits its use?
cards.back: It binds tubulin and so blocks granulocyte migration into the joint and the release of chemotactic factors and glycoprotein. It has no general analgesic or anti-inflammatory effect, and it does not change uric acid levels; its action is specific to gouty inflammation. Dose-related GI toxicity limits it, so it is second line to NSAIDs.

cards.front: What is the role of allopurinol in chronic gout, and what is its mechanism?
cards.back: Its metabolite alloxanthine is a long-acting, noncompetitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid synthesis. It is the first-choice drug for chronic gout, in both over-producers and under-excretors. It must not be started during an acute attack, and NSAID or colchicine cover is needed for 1 to 2 months.

cards.front: Short note: Colchicine in acute gout

points: Alkaloid of Colchicum autumnale
Binds tubulin and blocks granulocyte migration into the joint
Does not affect urate synthesis or excretion
Current regimen (GG14): 1.2 mg at the first sign of a flare, then 0.6 mg 1 hour later; works best within 24 h of onset
Older regimen (KDT): 0.5 mg every 1 to 3 hours, up to 4 doses a day, maximum 6 mg per course over 3 to 4 days; next course not before 3 to 7 days
Small doses at the first symptom may abort an attack
Low-dose prophylaxis while urate-lowering therapy is started
Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting and cramps are dose-limiting
Overdose: renal damage, CNS depression, bleeding, death from paralysis and respiratory failure
CYP3A4 inhibitors increase toxicity
Fastest-acting option for an acute attack
Second-line to NSAIDs because of higher toxicity

Febuxostat: non-purine, 40 mg up to 80 mg daily, maximum 120 mg/day; monitor liver function
Febuxostat carries a boxed warning of possible higher cardiovascular death than allopurinol (GG14)
Febuxostat is not combined with allopurinol, nor given with azathioprine or mercaptopurine

Needs adequate renal function; avoided in stone formers

Pegloticase: PEG-coupled recombinant uricase given IV every 2 weeks
Reserved for refractory gout; carries a risk of anaphylaxis
Never start during an acute attack
Cover with NSAID or colchicine for 1 to 2 months
Allopurinol is usually long term

cards.front: Classify: key toxicities of RA and gout drugs
cards.text: Hydroxychloroquine can cause {{retinal damage}}; sulfasalazine causes {{neutropenia}}; febuxostat needs liver monitoring for {{hepatotoxicity}}; allopurinol's rare but serious rash is {{Stevens-Johnson syndrome}}; pegloticase carries a risk of {{anaphylaxis}}.

cards.front: Which drugs interact with allopurinol and how?
cards.back: It inhibits xanthine oxidase so azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine doses must be cut to about a third (not thioguanine); it potentiates warfarin and theophylline; ampicillin rashes are commoner; probenecid and allopurinol alter each other's half-life. Febuxostat has the same azathioprine and theophylline caution.

cards.front: Essay: Gout - acute attack versus chronic hyperuricaemia

points: Normal plasma urate is about 2 to 6 mg/dL
Urate crystals deposit in joints, kidney and subcutaneous tissue (tophi)
Most patients under-excrete uric acid; drugs such as thiazides and furosemide can cause secondary hyperuricaemia
Treat with strong anti-inflammatory drugs without lowering urate
NSAIDs in high, quickly repeated doses, e.g. naproxen, indomethacin, piroxicam, diclofenac or etoricoxib
Colchicine is fastest but second-line because of toxicity
Intra-articular or systemic steroids when NSAIDs and colchicine are unsuitable
Continue NSAID at lower dose for 3 to 4 weeks after the attack
Start urate-lowering therapy once the attack subsides
Allopurinol is the first choice for over-producers and under-excretors
Probenecid is used for under-excretors with good renal function
Febuxostat as an alternative; pegloticase for refractory cases
Allopurinol and a uricosuric may be combined when the urate load is large
Tophi, nephropathy and deforming chronic arthritis
Long-term allopurinol can make tophi disappear and halt nephropathy

cards.front: Case: gout patient has recurrent tophi and renal stones. Choose urate-lowering therapy and cover.
cards.back: Allopurinol (first choice, works in over-producers and under-excretors, good for tophi and nephropathy); uricosurics are inappropriate with stones or low GFR. Febuxostat is an alternative if allopurinol fails, never combined. Refractory cases: pegloticase (uricase, anaphylaxis risk). Start only after the acute attack and cover 1 to 2 months with NSAID or colchicine.

cards.front: Short note: Selective COX-2 inhibitors - agents, status and safety

points: COX-2 is induced at inflamed sites; COX-1 keeps housekeeping functions
Coxibs do not inhibit platelet TXA2, so they do not block aggregation
Celecoxib, etoricoxib and parecoxib
Lumiracoxib (Europe only) suspended for hepatotoxicity
Rofecoxib withdrawn 2004 after cardiovascular event trials
Valdecoxib withdrawn 2005: MI after CABG and severe skin reactions
Lower endothelial PGI2 with no platelet effect: prothrombotic tilt
APC trial: about 2.5-fold more major CV events; CLASS trial showed no excess
2005 US committee: warning label, not full withdrawal
Only for patients at high risk of ulcer, perforation or bleed; lowest dose, shortest time
Avoid in ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease; do not add low-dose aspirin

cards.front: Short note: Clinically useful effects of aspirin

points: Headache, backache, myalgia, toothache, neuralgia, dysmenorrhoea
Effective at 0.3-0.6 g every 6-8 h; single-dose analgesia peaks near 1 g
Works in fever of any cause
Paracetamol usually preferred because it is safer
Acute rheumatic fever: first drug given; corticosteroids act faster
High doses (3-5 g/day) in RA; disease progression is not altered
Low dose (75-150 mg/day) after MI and in unstable angina
Reduces TIA and stroke; does not cut stroke risk after MI
Pre-eclampsia prevention: 80-100 mg/day from 12th week
Familial colonic polyposis; lower colon cancer incidence in regular users

cards.front: Short note: Aspirin intolerance (aspirin-sensitive asthma)

points: Susceptible people get asthma, angioneurotic swelling, urticaria or rhinitis after aspirin
Bronchospasm is the main danger in asthmatics
Chemically diverse NSAIDs provoke the same reaction
Cross-reactivity argues against an immune (allergic) basis
COX inhibition diverts arachidonic acid to the lipoxygenase (LT) pathway
Unproven
Avoid aspirin and other traditional NSAIDs
Nimesulide or a COX-2 inhibitor: most aspirin-sensitive asthmatics do not cross-react with nimesulide

cards.front: Short note: Steroid-sparing agents in rheumatoid arthritis

points: Corticosteroids act fast but do not stop joint destruction
Long-term steroid use causes serious harm, so the dose is kept low
Suppresses cell-mediated immunity, mainly T-cell and NK-cell function
Given with corticosteroids to spare steroid dose
Used mostly where systemic features are present
Not combined with methotrexate; 50-150 mg/day
Cyclosporine, chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide are rarely used in RA
Reserved for patients not responding to other DMARDs
Low dose (5-7.5 mg prednisolone) supplements NSAIDs; withdrawal is difficult
High dose for short periods in organ-threatening disease

cards.front: Essay: Recent advances in drug therapy of rheumatoid arthritis

points: RA is an autoimmune, chronic and progressive disease
NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not arrest it
Goals: remission, prevent erosions, preserve joint function
Methotrexate is the first-choice DMARD
Leflunomide, sulfasalazine, antimalarials and azathioprine as alternatives or add-ons
Advanced RA may need 2-3 DMARDs together
Tofacitinib: JAK-1 and JAK-3 inhibitor for severe RA not controlled by methotrexate
Not combined with azathioprine, cyclosporine or biologics
Anti-TNF agents: etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab
Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) after failure of one or more DMARDs
Abatacept and rituximab for RA not controlled by methotrexate plus an anti-TNF agent
Expensive; kept for severe refractory disease
Opportunistic infections, including TB and pneumocystis, are a major risk

cards.front: Short note: Management of gout - acute attack and prophylaxis

points: Treat the attack with strong anti-inflammatory drugs; do not lower urate during the attack
Start urate-lowering drug after the attack, with NSAID or colchicine cover
NSAIDs such as naproxen, piroxicam, diclofenac, indomethacin or etoricoxib; high early dose, lower dose for 3-4 weeks
Colchicine: fastest acting but more toxic; second-line
One or few joints: intra-articular triamcinolone
Systemic prednisolone if NSAIDs and colchicine are not usable
Allopurinol: first choice; for overproducers and under-excretors; tophi and nephropathy regress
Probenecid: second-line or adjunct; needs creatinine clearance above 50 ml/min and no renal stones
Febuxostat: alternative to allopurinol; not given together
Uricosurics with synthesis inhibitors when urate load is large
Attacks become more frequent in the first 1-2 months: cover with NSAID or colchicine
Liberal fluid intake during allopurinol therapy

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacotherapy of osteoarthritis

points: Drugs give symptomatic relief of pain and stiffness
Choice depends on pain severity, risk factors and response
Paracetamol: first-choice analgesic for most patients
Topical NSAIDs for mild to moderate knee or hand OA, as initial or adjunct therapy
Aspirin is used infrequently now
Propionic acid derivatives, diclofenac, aceclofenac, meloxicam or nimesulide are used
Lowest effective dose; lower dose in the elderly
High GI risk: coxib, or a proton pump inhibitor with the NSAID
Hypertension or CV risk: avoid coxibs; use a propionic acid derivative or aspirin at the lowest dose
Aceclofenac enhances glycosaminoglycan synthesis (proposed cartilage protection)

cards.front: Short note: TNF inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis

points: TNF acts on TNFR1 and TNFR2 on T-cells and macrophages
Soluble receptor (etanercept) or antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) neutralise TNF
Suppress macrophage and T-cell function; joint inflammation regresses and new erosions slow
Etanercept: TNF-receptor-Fc fusion protein; 25-50 mg s.c. once or twice weekly
Infliximab: chimeric monoclonal antibody; 3-5 mg/kg IV every 4-8 weeks
Adalimumab: human monoclonal antibody; 40 mg s.c. every 2 weeks
Certolizumab and golimumab are other TNF inhibitors
Opportunistic infections, including TB and pneumocystis pneumonia
Infliximab: infusion reactions; can worsen heart failure
Etanercept: injection-site reactions; more chest infections
Generally added to methotrexate when response to it is inadequate or disease is progressing fast
Methotrexate co-therapy improves response and reduces antibody formation

cards.front: Why does diclofenac not block low-dose aspirin's cardioprotection, but ibuprofen does?
cards.back: Diclofenac spares COX-1 and has no appreciable antiplatelet action. Ibuprofen occupies the active serine of COX-1 reversibly and so blocks aspirin's irreversible acetylation.

cards.front: Why is naproxen suited to acute gout?
cards.back: It is a potent anti-inflammatory that inhibits leucocyte migration into the joint. Its long half-life (12-16 h) allows twice-daily dosing. Dose: 750 mg stat, then 250 mg 8-hourly until the attack subsides. With regular use it suppresses platelet function.

cards.front: Why have phenylbutazone and oxyphenbutazone gone out of use?
cards.back: Both are potent anti-inflammatories with slow onset, but they carry high gastric toxicity, Na+ and water retention, CNS and hypersensitivity reactions, hypothyroidism, and residual risk of bone-marrow depression.

cards.front: Piroxicam: why once-daily dosing, and why is it not a first-choice NSAID?
cards.back: Its plasma half-life is about 2 days, so steady state takes about a week and once-daily dosing is enough. Its GI and skin toxicity and oedema are relatively high, so it is not a first choice for any condition.

cards.front: Parenteral ketorolac: where is it used, and what restricts it?
cards.back: Used for post-operative, dental and acute musculoskeletal pain, renal colic, migraine and bone-metastasis pain. Not for preanaesthetic or obstetric analgesia, not for OA or RA, and not with anticoagulants. Oral use beyond 5 days is not advised.

cards.front: How does nabumetone spare the gastric mucosa?
cards.back: Nabumetone is a prodrug. Its active COX inhibitor (6-methoxy naphthyl acetic acid) forms in the tissues after absorption, not in the gastric mucosa.

cards.front: Mephenamic acid: which pain is it used for, and what is its main adverse effect?
cards.back: Muscle, joint and soft-tissue pain, and dysmenorrhoea, where strong anti-inflammatory action is not needed. The main adverse effect is dose-related diarrhoea; haemolytic anaemia is rare but serious.

cards.front: Which injury and procedural uses are listed for ibuprofen and its congeners?
cards.back: Soft-tissue injury, fractures, vasectomy, tooth extraction, and post-operative and post-partum swelling and pain, where inflammation is less prominent than pain.

cards.front: Ketoprofen and flurbiprofen compared with ibuprofen: what is the trade-off?
cards.back: Ketoprofen has similar anti-inflammatory efficacy but more side effects. Flurbiprofen is more effective but causes more gastric side effects.

cards.front: Why is meloxicam called a preferential COX-2 inhibitor, and is it gentler on the stomach?
cards.back: Its COX-2/COX-1 selectivity is about 10:1, yet it still measurably reduces platelet TXA2 at therapeutic doses. GI side effects are milder than piroxicam's, but ulcer complications occur on long use, and there is no convincing evidence it is safer than other NSAIDs.

cards.front: Etodolac: what sets it apart in clinical use?
cards.back: A moderately COX-2-selective indole acetic acid with better GI tolerance at lower doses. Post-operative analgesia lasts 6-8 h. Approved for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and acute musculoskeletal pain.

cards.front: Which diclofenac congener has a proposed cartilage-protective action, and by what mechanism?
cards.back: Aceclofenac, which is a moderately COX-2-selective congener of diclofenac. It enhances glycosaminoglycan synthesis, which is the proposed chondroprotective action.

cards.front: Acute rheumatic fever: which drug is given first, and when are others added?
cards.back: Aspirin is the first drug in all cases. Other drugs are added or substituted only if aspirin fails or the disease is severe. Corticosteroids act faster.

cards.front: Why does colchicine not lower blood urate, and what does it do?
cards.back: It does not inhibit uric acid synthesis or increase its excretion, and it is neither analgesic nor anti-inflammatory in general. It binds tubulin and blocks granulocyte migration into the joint, cutting the release of chemotactic factors and the aggravating glycoprotein.

cards.front: Why do acute attacks become more frequent in the first 1-2 months of urate-lowering therapy?
cards.back: Fluctuating plasma urate makes crystals repeatedly dissolve and re-form in the joints. Cover with NSAID or colchicine for this period. Urate-lowering drugs are not started during an acute attack.

cards.front: Acute gout when NSAIDs are unsuitable: which steroid options exist?
cards.back: One or a few joints: intra-articular triamcinolone (10 mg in small joints, 30 mg in wrist). Systemic: prednisolone 40-60 mg for one day, then tapered over 1-2 weeks, for renal failure or previous peptic ulcer bleed. Colchicine is second-line.

cards.front: Febuxostat: class, use and key cautions
cards.back: A non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, as effective as or better than allopurinol. Start 40 mg OD, up to 80 mg (max 120 mg/day). Not combined with allopurinol, though they can be given in sequence. Not for malignancy-associated hyperuricaemia. Liver damage is the key adverse effect; avoid with mercaptopurine, azathioprine or theophylline.

cards.front: Pegloticase: what is it and when is it used?
cards.back: A recombinant uricase, coupled to methoxy-PEG, that converts urate to soluble allantoin. Given IV every 2 weeks, only for rare refractory symptomatic gout. It is immunogenic, causes infusion reactions including anaphylaxis, and the response is lost in many patients.

cards.front: Lesinurad: what kind of drug is it and how is it used?
cards.back: A newer uricosuric with a mechanism similar to probenecid. Approved as a treatment option alone or with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

cards.front: How do inflammatory cells worsen an acute gout attack?
cards.back: They engulf urate crystals and release chemotactic factors that recruit granulocytes. Lactic acid lowers local pH and promotes more crystal precipitation. Lysosomal enzymes damage joint tissue, and a glycoprotein aggravates inflammation.

cards.front: Low-dose corticosteroid in RA: what is its main drawback?
cards.back: Prednisolone 5-7.5 mg supplements NSAIDs and gives prompt relief, but it cannot arrest the disease. Withdrawal is hard: flares occur and the patient becomes steroid-dependent.

cards.front: Aspirin and COX: fill the blanks
cards.text: Aspirin inhibits COX by {{acetylating}} a {{serine}} residue; the platelet effect lasts about {{one week}}, which matches platelet turnover time.

cards.front: Allopurinol: fill the blanks
cards.text: Allopurinol inhibits {{xanthine oxidase}}; its long-acting metabolite {{alloxanthine}} is mainly responsible for inhibiting uric acid synthesis in vivo.

cards.front: Probenecid: fill the blanks
cards.text: Probenecid blocks {{organic acid}} transport in the renal {{tubule}}, and so inhibits the reabsorption of urate by the transporter {{URAT-1}}.

cards.front: Colchicine: fill the blanks
cards.text: Colchicine binds {{tubulin}} and blocks granulocyte migration into the joint; prophylactic maintenance is {{0.5-1 mg/day}} for {{4-8 weeks}}.

cards.front: Indomethacin in patent ductus arteriosus: fill the blanks
cards.text: Indomethacin closes the ductus in most cases with {{three}} IV injections, given {{12-hourly}}, each of {{0.1-0.2 mg/kg}}.
